title: Keizan's Zazen Yojinki, Part 1
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett's main teaching emphasizes the importance of cultivating awareness and presence in every moment, rather than getting caught up in thoughts or distractions about life, death, or external circumstances. By practicing Zazen (meditation), we can develop a mind and body that are free from thinking and acting, allowing for clarity and inner peace. This freedom is not just an individual experience, but also extends to all beings, including ourselves and others, when we sit still and accept our experiences with an open heart.

sentences.text: Good morning, everybody.
If you noticed the little directory of talks and saw that Kanshin Allison Tait was giving the talk today, you might have noticed I'm not Allison.
Allison's a little too sick, sadly.
She'll be okay, I hope, but she wasn't up for giving a talk.
So I want to thank Xu Dou, Chris, for giving the talk yesterday.
Thank you very much.
Isn't it great to be plunged into the wonderful mythology of Buddha's awakening?
This wonderful land.
And I know Chris, like me, finds the quirky language of the Pali Canon kind of like soul food.
It's an acquired taste, I guess, but I enjoyed it.
Hopefully everybody else did.
But what I really benefited from, besides that, were Chris's remarks right before she read that long quotation about Buddha's awakening.
She said that we humans seem to need occasions to remember our intentions, and Rohatsu is such a powerful occasion to remember our intention, how we want to live, how we want to practice.
Her talking about that made me think that it is true in the usual way of an occasion: this is an annual remembrance, and Buddha was a historical figure from long ago.
He did inspiring practice, heroic practice, and we can take inspiration from that to renew our own practice.
That's true.
But I was thinking that's too small of a vision, really.
Somehow Chris talking about that helped me feel into how it's not just that.
It's also that Buddha is sitting with us right now.
He has no problem with Zoom.
We're here because Buddha is practicing with us, and Buddha exists because we're practicing.
It's not some long-ago thing that somehow led to us getting lucky later and doing a sort of pale imitation of that great earlier work.
It's more that we and Buddha are awakening together in this Rohatsu, like we do every time.
And in between Rohatsus too, always awakening together with Buddha.
How easy it is to lose track of that, isn't it?
We all do.
It's kind of sad too, because it made me realize that when I lose track of that, I'm doing a kind of othering, you know what I mean?
I'm making Buddha into an other, and I'm even making myself, each of us making ourselves, into an other.
There's the ordinary one who suffers and the one who gets inspired.
We're all separated and divided, and in our division and our separation is our suffering, right?
So maybe we can take some inspiration from Rohatsu and Chris's encouragement and let those others come back home, come back together.
All of ourselves and all of our Buddhas, all of it is right here, practicing right here.
Such thoughts always make me think of this poem from Katagiri Roshi.
If you've heard it a hundred times, a hundred and one is the perfect number.
This poem was found in Katagiri Roshi's papers after he died.
He never published it.
And maybe I'm especially thinking about Katagiri Roshi because he led the first Rohatsu I ever did, which was the first sesshin I ever did.
I did the math.
I had to get my calculator.
It was 34 years ago, bizarrely.
So here's Katagiri Roshi.
*This peaceful life.
Being told that it is impossible, one believes in despair.
Is that so?
Being told that it is possible, one believes in excitement.
That's right.
But whichever is chosen, it does not fit one's heart neatly.*
*Being asked what is unfitting, I don't know what it is.
But my heart knows somehow.
I feel irresistible desire to know.
What a mystery a human is.
As to this mystery, clarifying, knowing how to live, knowing how to walk with people, demonstrating and teaching this is the Buddha.
And from my human eyes, I feel it's impossible to become Buddha.
But this I, regarding what the Buddha does, vows to aspire, to practice, to be resolute.
Tells myself, yes I will.
Just practice right here now.*
*Achieve continuity endlessly, forever.
This is living in vow.
Here is one's peaceful life found.*
Isn't that beautiful and humble?
This very senior teacher, one of the founders of American Soto Zen, at the end of his life saying, "I don't get it, but there's a feeling here.
My heart knows somehow."
My heart knows somehow.
So I'll keep practicing.
Impossible to be Buddha.
But we are Buddha.
So let's return to Great Master Keizan.
His story and his teachings are important, I think.
It's good that he's popped up.
I want to share with you just a short encyclopedia entry.
We'll get a little academic, though it's a Buddhist encyclopedia.
This is William Bodiford's entry in the Gale Encyclopedia on Buddhism.
I'll try to skip some of the nitty-gritty, but it's good to get a little context.
Keizan lived 1264 to 1325.
So he was born about a decade after Dogen died.
He didn't study with Dogen, but he studied Zen directly with four of Dogen's leading disciples: Eijo, Jakuin, Jian, and Jikai.
He succeeded Jikai as the second abbot of Daijouji monastery, which is just a hop, skip, and a jump away from Eiji.
I got to visit there one time.
As Chris mentioned, Keizan was never an abbot of Eiji.
He actually followed his teacher Jikai to this other monastery not too far away,
which is a whole other complicated story, and ended up being the abbot there.
Then he founded a new monastery in Noto province called Yokoji, which he saw as the future HQ.
So he had ambition way back then.
This was to be the headquarters temple for Soto Zen.
From there he founded six more monasteries nearby, and as I mentioned yesterday, many of his students also founded more monasteries.
So here's the beginning of a proliferation.
In terms of actual temples, it built up even further a couple of generations later, but more than Dogen, he was an organizer and a creator of temples.
Bodiford goes on to say:
*Keizan worked hard to establish a firm religious and institutional basis for the nascent, the new Soto Zen school.
So he authored a history of Soto Zen, founded a memorial hall at his temple, Yokoji, to enshrine relics of the first five generations of patriarchs.
He wrote beginner's guides to Zen training, and detailed instructions for every aspect of Zen monastic life.*
He also came up with a way of rotating the abbotship, rotating the abbots between pure monasteries, which was important and helped prevent fighting.
Humans are always fighting, so he tried to avoid some of that with systemic thinking.
In another piece, I'm going in and out of Bodiford, but in another piece, Bodiford writes that Keizan was not a great writer.
He wasn't inspiring and lofty and philosophical like Dogen, but he was practical.
He figured stuff out and he wrote stuff down.
Later, they artificially made it sound like Keizan and Dogen were different camps, that Dogen was the pure one and Keizan was the practical one.
But Bodiford says here, not so much.
They were both deeply religious figures, really centered on formal practice.
But then, in addition to Zen training and monasticism, Keizan broadened things spiritually too, so organizationally and spiritually.
Here's what Bodiford wrote in the encyclopedia:
*Keizan was a man of his times.
In addition to Zen history, Zen training, and Zen monasticism, his writings reveal many religious themes common to other 14th century Japanese.
Keizan openly described, for example, his reliance on inspired dreams as a source of religious authority.
His use of astrology, his devotion to his mother and grandmother, his invocation of the local gods who protect Buddhism, and his devout faith in the Bodhisattva Avalokiteshvara, Kannon.

These kinds of transectarian religious values exerted, no doubt, greater influence on the lives of ordinary people than his description of the difficult Zen practice, Zen doctrine, and Zen monastic forms.*
So he wrote about things important to ordinary people.
And Keizan's surviving writings constitute a prime source for the study of medieval Japanese religiosity and the ways that it interacted with other traditions.
A lot of his writings got lost, the originals lost, and now we have copies of copies of copies, and there are lots of mistakes.
But scholars, Bodiford said, agree on a few major works that were definitely written by him.
Denko Roku, which is the history of stories of the enlightenments in the lineage.
Denko Roku.
Zazen Yojinki, that we're looking at this week, on practicing zazen.

And then a couple of monastic manuals: Tokoku Gyoji Jijo, the procedures at Tokoku Monastery, which is also known as Keizan Shingi, Keizan's regulations; and Tokuki, the chronicle of Tokoku Monastery.
For the last one, he has a whole other piece describing how important it was to write histories.
Writing the history of your monastery enshrined it for future generations as an important example.
So our messy website will have to do, I guess, until we get a historian going.
Anyway, I thought you'd like a little context there about Keizan and his importance.
So let's go back to his text about zazen, Zazen Yojinki.
Next paragraph.
*Mind originally is undifferentiated, undivided, and the body manifests various forms.
Mind only and body only cannot be explained in terms of sameness or difference.
Mind transforms itself and becomes body, and the manifest body as different forms.
Mind transforms itself, becomes body, and the manifest body as different forms.
When one wave is generated, 10,000 waves appear.
When mental discrimination arises, 10,000 dharmas appear.
The four elements and the five skandhas interdependently originate, and the four limbs and the five senses become manifest.
Furthermore, the 36 parts of the body and the 12 conditions ceaselessly continue to appear.*
Don't worry about that part too much.
*In explaining the interdependence of phenomena, the mind can be compared to ocean water and the body to waves.
In explaining the interdependence of phenomena, the mind can be compared to ocean water and the body to waves.
There are no waves without water and no water without waves.
Water and waves are inseparable.
Motion and stillness are indistinguishable.
Therefore, it is said, the true person who comprehends life and death, coming and going, realizes the imperishable body of the four elements and the five skandhas.*
Here's that last part again.

Once you understand this water and waves analogy, then you are a true person who comprehends life and death, coming and going, and realizes the imperishable body of the four elements and the five skandhas.
This whole paragraph is really interesting.
It's a lovely meditation, isn't it, on the body-mind?
How they generate each other, how the whole thing starts and proliferates, how to understand it.
And it's yet another way of saying not two.
We were talking about that the other day.
The body-mind and body do appear to be different, and yet they're not really different.
A wave looks different from the whole ocean, but you can't separate them, right?
And the central wave here is my life, your life, our life, Buddha's life.
We're born when a wave arises in the ocean, and that's a temporary thing.
Sooner or later, the wave returns to the ocean: birth and death.
Dogen said the exact same stuff this morning in Genjokoan.
Remember all that?
Our life and death is like firewood and ash.
It's like winter and spring.
It's like waves in the ocean.
You can't have firewood without ash, but they aren't exactly the same or different either.
You can't have spring without winter.
They appear to be different, right?
But are they?
Where's the boundary?
How can you really tell?
So can we rest in zazen in this way?
That's what he's saying.
We can rest in zazen with an appreciation for waves and stillness, body and mind, manifestations coming and going.
And we're in the center of it all.
It's such a mystery.
What a mystery this being human is, Katagiri said.
I think one of the obvious places you can really see the mystery of being human, or the mystery of life and death, is looking at a body right after death.
Not all of us have had many opportunities to do that, because we're so death-averse that we whisk the bodies away.
In our dualistic way, we tend to think of the mind as a force that makes the body alive, right?
Then once we die, the mind is gone, or it goes somewhere else.
It goes to heaven, depending what you think about.
It gets reborn, goes to the bardos.
And then there's just this thing called body.
But I don't know if that really makes sense.
The experience of this thing we call a body is just so different from this thing we call a body after death.
It's hard to even describe if you haven't experienced this directly, and I'm sure we all have different ways of experiencing it too, but it's so interesting and shocking.
What is this ocean without waves, when the wave subsides?
After Talus's wife Diane died, he put out a picture of her no longer alive body.
They'd already cleaned and dressed her and put some flowers around her.
I think she had a rakusu on.
It was interesting to me how hard it was to look at that photo.
I felt this aversion.
The part of me that wants to hold onto these simple notions of life and death was really disturbed and confused.
What is that?
I saved it on the computer, but I didn't want to look at it.
And then later I made myself sit with Diane's body in that way.
Breathe.
Powerful.
So there's something here for us: Zazen is a vehicle of exploration.
Something about life and death, something about body and mind.
We have this simple story, but it's clearly not true.
What is it?
What are we?
What is it to breathe and be, to sit in Zazen and then to stand up and then one day to not be alive?
What is it?
And in case you weren't here this morning, I want to mention that we're practicing with this today, actually.
A few of us directly, a few of us indirectly.
Right now our sangha friend Ann Mikkelsen's not alive body.
I think we need a different word than body for that, you know?
Anyway, her body is in the morgue this morning, and soon they're going to load it up into the mortuary van, which they have all figured out how to do.
It's incredibly hard to carry lifeless bodies around, too.
They're heavier, somehow.
It's very mysterious, this whole thing.
And they're going to take Ann's body to the crematorium, and Edie and I are going to meet them there this afternoon with a few family members.
It has to be really tiny because of COVID, so I'm sorry we can't have more of us there.
And we're going to call out to Ann.
We're going to lay her on a table right next to the door of the crematorium, right by the oven, and we're going to call out to her and we're going to chant with her.
We're going to encourage her to return to Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha.
We're going to call on the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas to help out, to help us, to help her.

We're going to call especially on the Bodhisattva of Compassion, of whom Keizan, we just learned, was a big fan of Kannon, by chanting the Enmei Jukku Kannon Gyo, the first sutra for Kannon, for Avalokiteshvara.

And in the middle of this little ceremony (it's not a long ceremony, I don't remember how old, how many years Ann got to be on this planet, 79 maybe, something like that) this little ceremony just takes half an hour.

In the middle, the body is slid into the oven on rollers, and as the officiant, I'll shout out as loud as I can so that they can hear it in all the worlds: "Now fire, heat up, complete this existence."

And as the ovens and fires transform this Rupa, right, this matter, this not alive body, from what looks like Ann, kind of, not really, into ash that we can put in an urn, we'll chant the Heart Sutra.

We'll chant the Heart Sutra to remind ourselves and remind Ann's spirit, whatever you want to call it, how wonderful it is, right, how wonderful it all is that everything is empty, free, fluid, interpenetrated, right, the wondrous nature of emptiness.

And at the very end of all that, and the oven will still be roaring, it takes a couple of hours, Edie will call out, "We offer the merit of our chanting to you, Ann Mikkelsen, dear friend, returning to your origin.
We pray that wherever you are, your world may be beautiful."
So you'll be with us in spirit for sure.
So these big passings are powerful, right?
It's just powerful just hearing about that, right?
And I'm sure many of us are thinking about people we've lost.
Yeah, it's powerful, it is.
It's wonderful, it's sad, it's deep.
And when you're contemplating these things, don't you think it's like deep meditation?
Because you can't be anywhere else, right?
You really can only be right here, sitting with someone as they die.
You're not thinking about the laundry, you know?
You can't.
You can only be deeply, deeply present and deeply in love.
So these big passings are so powerful that they anchor us and we feel that.
But I think what Keizan is trying to tell us about Zazen is, back to this idea, don't other yourself the rest of the time.
We can practice, we can train, we can orient our hearts so that every moment of our life is just like that.
It is this mysterious body-mind wave crashing on the shore.
Like you can't miss it.
Every moment is like, wow!
No moment is ordinary, every moment extraordinary, or extraordinary in its ordinariness.
Because waves and water are beautiful, but they're also just waves and water, you know?
Three-quarters of the Earth's surface or something is ocean.
Us little landlocked primitive beings who can't breathe underwater are like, oh, look at that.
The world is vast, you know?
And in that paragraph I mentioned there's lots of little Buddhist lists.
Do you notice all that?
I said don't worry about that too much, but that's Buddhist talk for saying this includes everything.
The spirit of aliveness, of immediacy, of the bigness of everything, the vastness.
It includes everything we can experience, everything we conceive, everything we can know, and everything we can't know, everything.
So a period of zazen, even if our conscious mind isn't always quite tuned into this with our thinking, every period of zazen can be just the same as sliding Ann Mikkelsen's body into the oven.
Just that.
No words, right?
No words.
There's no words for that moment.
So let's do a few more paragraphs.
That maybe feels like enough, but I have an agenda.
I'll read a little more.
I'm kind of curious about getting through this whole text by the end of the week.
We'll see.
It's fun to say:
*Practicing zazen is directly entering into the ocean of Buddha nature and manifesting the body of all Buddhas.
The fundamental purity of the radiant mind is disclosed.
The original brightness shines forth without limit, just like there's no increase or decrease in the waters of the ocean, and the waves are never distracted in their course.
All Buddhas appear in the world for the single-minded function of causing sentient beings to realize Buddhahood and attain this manifest enlightenment.
Their incomparably tranquil and wondrous technique is known as zazen, also known as the self-fulfilling samadhi, or the king of all samadhis.*
[unclear: "Stokin"] wrote about that too.
It's basically just saying what I tried to say a little more eloquently there.
Entering into the ocean deeply.
*And if you abide tranquilly in samadhi, it directly enlightens the primordial mind and is the true gate to the attainment of the way of the Buddhas.

If you wish to attain, if you wish to enlighten this primordial mind, renounce discriminative knowledge and interpretation,* stop interpreting, *cast away the distinctions between worldly and Buddhist principles,* don't make this so special, *and remove all attachments.* No problem.
*And manifest the one true mind.
Then the clouds of delusion will be dispersed and the mind will be as clear as the new moon.*
*The Buddha said, "Listening and thinking are standing outside the gate.
Zazen is sitting calmly in one's own home."* Isn't that great?
*Listening and thinking are standing outside the gate.
Zazen is sitting calmly in one's own home.* How true is this, how true?
*For listening and thinking perpetuate one-sided views, leaving the primordial mind in turmoil, just like being outside the gate.
But Zazen creates an all-pervasive restfulness, sitting calmly at home.* Sitting calmly at home.
So, how do we make up all that?
It all sounds great.
There's a lot more to go in the text, which we'll get to.

But after this lovely talk ends, at least I hope you're experiencing it in some positive way, I hope so, after this talk, lovely or not, ends, you'll sit down again in Zazen, and won't it just all start up again?
Right?
My shoulder hurts.
What am I going to do about my sister?
I can't believe she voted for Trump.
Is it too cold out for a walk?
It's sunny at least.
Dang, I'm no good at Zazen.
Did I remember to send that work email on Tuesday?
Shit!
Blah, blah, blah, blah, blah, right?
This does not sound like all this stuff he's talking about.
Radiant, tranquil, peaceful, free, you know.
So, how do we work with this?
Well, we're almost out of time, so we'll say more tomorrow, and you already know plenty.
You already know what you need to know.
It's not like there's some secret that I'll reveal to you later.
That's the secret of Dharma: there's no secrets.
Do you know that?
But we also heard in another Zen text, which we'll chant tomorrow morning actually, that it's just a hair's breadth deviation that we're out of attunement.
We do know all this stuff, and so it's not like we need to sign up for a Ph.D. in Buddhist studies and write a long thesis on Keizan to get it, all you could.
It's more a matter of attunement, right?

And patience and support, helping each other as we walk, Katagiri Roshi saying, I just want to learn how to walk with people, feeling each other's presence as we each do our best, breath after breath, step after step.
It sure helps to drop out of our heads a little bit, so when you sit down, you can make a conscious effort to not try to stop the blah, blah, blah.
Good luck with that, right?
But to invite the energy to just drop.
Try it now.
Close your eyes if you want.
Give yourself a little adjustment, a little self-love there.
Maybe you can drop your awareness out of the head, more into the heart, the center of the chest, the belly.
I was listening to this great early meditation by Stephen Levine about the belly, and the belly being soft.
He's saying every tension and problem arises when the belly is tight, you know?
So can the belly be soft?
Maybe that's the real key.
So it's body and mind.
It's not something we can figure out, remember the right tips or rules or the clever teachings.
It's experiential.
It's ground up.
It takes a long time for those waves to pass across the ocean.
We have time.
But we also don't have time.
The wave is going to crash into the shore really soon, too.
So dear Dharma friends, let's really appreciate our practice and not trivialize it because it's only over Zoom, or it's of this schedule or that schedule, or my cat or my dog is bugging me.
There's some interesting images going on.
Occasionally I look up and go, "Hi puppy."
But even with all this, especially with all this, we're not conditioned on having a beautiful quiet zendo.
As much as we love that and we hope to have that again, watching the light move across the zendo floor, well, you know what?
The light's moving across your floor at home today, too.
You just have to notice that we have this powerful, powerful gift from Dogen, from Keizan, from all the ancestors who are not before, right?
They are here now.

And the woman ancestors, Keizan's mother and grandmother, his patron, too, was a woman, and he wrote a lot about how much he loved these three women, all the ancestors, the animal ancestors, all the ancestors.
They're here to help you.
And they depend on you.
So there's a big responsibility to this practice.
But it's not a heavy responsibility.
It's not crushing.
How could a wave be crushed?
Waves aren't crushable.
They're fluid.
And yet it's what we all chose, somehow.
I don't know why you chose this.
I don't know why I did.
I was talking to somebody about that in Dokusan.
He was like, "I don't know how to explain this.
Why am I into this?"
And I said, "I don't know either.
I don't know either."
And yet we're doing an essential function.
Dogen said, who would take wasteful delight in the spark from the flintstone?
Somehow that Flintstone got sparked for every one of us.
And no matter how that looks in your life, whether you are like a lifer and put on lots of robes or not, it doesn't matter.
For now, you're alive.
For now, you have the Alive Mind Body.
And that Alive Mind Body can heal you and heal the world through Zazen.
That's what Keizan's saying.
And I guess we agree with him.
Here's one last little quotation for now.
I think this is Keizan.
I indented it like a quotation, but I can't remember now.
Looks good, though.
*The most important concern is that the mind be free from thinking and the body be free from acting.*
Yeah, this is Keizan.
*When distracting relations are ended, mental disturbances are subdued.
When mental disturbances are subdued, the unchanging body is manifest.
And you continually realize its clarity as neither extinction nor commotion.*
So we'll unpack that tomorrow.
There's a lot of technical language there, but the point being what I was saying before that.
I don't know if that helped to throw in a Buddhist quote.
Sometimes these beautiful teachers just confuse us.
Have you noticed that?
Mind that's free from thinking means a mind that is free, even as it's thinking.
That's the thing.
Don't worry about the thinking.
But feel the freedom.
And I want to suggest that you especially may be able to feel that freedom in your body as you sit in stillness, deep stillness, released, relaxed, accepting.
Even when there's pain and discomfort or you're upset, it's okay.
The ocean doesn't get upset.
It's just the surface gets a little rippled sometimes.
You can be big enough to let those ripples come and go as we sit together.
Attention equally extend to every being.
